title: Long-running work: the MCP Tasks pattern

concept.heading: Return a durable handle now; let the work finish whether or not anyone is watching
paragraphs: Reconciling a month means reading every donor's gifts, which on a real CRM is minutes. A tool that blocks for minutes fails the first time a laptop sleeps, a free host restarts, or a browser tab closes, and the staff member never learns whether it finished. The fix is a task: create a row in SQLite with status working, start the work in a background thread, and return the task id at once.

The client polls get_task(task_id) until the status is completed or failed, and the result is on the row. Because the state is in the database and the thread lives in the server process, a client that disconnects can come back, or a different client can take over, and finish the poll. The 2026-07-28 spec standardizes this as the tasks extension with tasks/get; the SDK's support is still settling, so this lesson implements the same pattern as two ordinary tools that every host can already call.

Two details carry the weight: a failure inside the thread must land on the row as status failed with the error text, never vanish; and the thread must not hold a connection open across the whole job. Each donor is its own short call.
concept.lowCodeEquivalent: A long-running flow started by a child-flow call that returns immediately, with the parent checking a status row in Dataverse. Or an Azure Durable Function status endpoint. The handle-and-poll shape is the same.

pythonBlock.title: Python you need: threading.Thread, daemon threads, try/except around the whole job
pythonBlock.intro: A daemon thread does not keep the process alive on exit. The try/except is what turns a crash into a failed row instead of a silent loss.
pythonBlock.code:
import threading

def run_in_background(self, task_id, fn, *args):
    def job():
        try:
            self.complete(task_id, fn(*args))
        except Exception as e:                       # noqa: BLE001 - the row IS the error report
            self.fail(task_id, f"{e.__class__.__name__}: {e}")
    t = threading.Thread(target=job, name=f"task-{task_id}", daemon=True)
    t.start()
    return t
